title: How the Body Works
description: How the body's main systems work and how they fit together, from cells and tissues to the heart, lungs, gut, kidneys, nerves, hormones and the immune system. Each lesson pairs a mechanism with a practical health link, such as what a blood pressure reading means or how a vaccine works, and none of it is personal medical advice.
audience: A curious adult with no biology since school who wants to understand what their own body is doing and to read health information with confidence. They need everyday arithmetic and nothing else. The course does not diagnose, treat or advise any individual, and it does not replace a conversation with a doctor, nurse or pharmacist.
outcomes: You'll be able to name the four basic tissues and say how one fertilised egg gives rise to many kinds of cell.
You'll be able to explain homeostasis and trace a negative feedback loop for temperature and for blood pressure.
You'll be able to follow blood through the heart and calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume.
You'll be able to read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic and say why one reading is not a diagnosis.
You'll be able to explain how air moves in and out, how oxygen reaches the blood, and how to read a respiratory rate against the normal ranges.
You'll be able to follow food through the alimentary canal and work out an energy budget and the WHO's sugar and salt limits.
You'll be able to use the 180 litres and 99 percent figures to find daily urine volume and say what ADH does.
You'll be able to read a nerve signal from a voltage trace and trace a reflex arc.
You'll be able to explain how insulin and glucagon hold blood glucose steady and what changes in type 2 diabetes.
You'll be able to separate innate from adaptive immunity, say what a vaccine does, and read a vaccination coverage figure.

modules.title: Building blocks and balance
modules.summary: Cells, tissues, the idea of a steady internal state, and the bones and muscles that show how use shapes tissue.

modules.title: Circulation, breathing and digestion
modules.summary: How blood is pumped and measured, how air and food are taken in, and how oxygen and nutrients reach the blood.

modules.title: Energy, balance and control
modules.summary: How food becomes energy, how the kidneys, nerves and hormones keep the body steady, and how the immune system and vaccines protect it.

lessons.title: Cells and tissues
lessons.objective: Name the four basic tissue types, say how one fertilised egg gives rise to many kinds of cell, and explain why a failure of the controls on cell division matters for health.

concepts.title: Differentiation
concepts.summary: Early, unspecialised cells become specialised in structure and function as the body develops from a single fertilised egg.

concepts.title: Tissue
concepts.summary: Cells of one kind or a few kinds organised into layers that do one job; the body has four broad categories: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.

concepts.title: Stem cell
concepts.summary: An unspecialised cell that can divide without limit as needed and can, under specific conditions, differentiate into specialised cells.

concepts.title: Cell cycle control
concepts.summary: Internal and external stop and advance signals decide when a cell divides; loss of that control can lead to cancer.

misconceptions: Learners picture one kind of generic cell. The body has at least 200 distinct cell types that share essentially the same internal structures and differ in shape and job.
Learners think epithelium means skin only. It also lines internal cavities and passageways and forms glands.

Learners think cancer is something that enters the body. It starts from the body's own cells when the controls on division fail, and the immune system often removes such cells before they cause trouble.
sequence: One fertilised egg, trillions of cells: where the variety comes from.
Form follows job: at least 200 cell types, same internal parts, different shapes.
Cells in layers: the four tissue categories and what each is for.
Stem cells as the source of new specialised cells.
Dividing under control: stop and advance signals, and what loss of control can mean, including the difference between a benign and a malignant tumour.
examples: Epithelium covers the outside of the body, lines passageways and forms glands, so a sheet of tightly packed cells on a surface is epithelial.
Muscle tissue is excitable and contracts to produce movement, while nervous tissue carries electrochemical signals between regions of the body.
A tissue sample from the cervix is used in OpenStax to show how orderly layered tissue looks and how that organisation breaks down in cancer (describe in words; do not reproduce the micrograph).

figures.shows: Four panels of simple tissue drawings (a sheet, fibres in a matrix, long contractile cells, a branched cell), each unlabelled, with a switchable view that adds the tissue name and one job.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each name onto the panel it belongs to, then open the labelled view to check.

figures.shows: Tissue, one job, one place in the body, for the four tissues.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: A sample under the microscope shows flat sheets of tightly packed cells that line the inside of a passageway. Which tissue category is this?
questionPlan.answer: Epithelial

questionPlan.sample: Sort each job into the tissue that does it: lines a passageway; binds organs together; contracts to move bones; carries nerve impulses; covers the outside of the body.
questionPlan.answer: Epithelial: lines a passageway, covers the outside of the body. Connective: binds organs together. Muscle: contracts to move bones. Nervous: carries nerve impulses.

questionPlan.sample: Which statement fits the textbook account of how cancer arises?
choices: Stop and advance signals that control cell division fail, so cells keep dividing
A cell type that the body does not normally make enters from outside
Tissues lose their blood supply and the cells turn abnormal
questionPlan.answer: Stop and advance signals that control cell division fail, so cells keep dividing

questionPlan.sample: An unspecialised cell that can divide without limit and, under the right conditions, become specialised is called a ___ cell.
questionPlan.answer: stem

lessons.title: Keeping the body steady
lessons.objective: Explain homeostasis as a dynamic balance kept by feedback, trace a negative feedback loop for body temperature and for blood pressure, and tell negative from positive feedback.

concepts.title: Homeostasis
concepts.summary: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life.

concepts.title: Negative feedback
concepts.summary: A response that opposes the change that set it off, so a value is held within a narrow range.

concepts.title: Positive feedback
concepts.summary: A response that adds to the change that set it off, as with oxytocin and labour contractions.

concepts.title: Baroreceptor reflex
concepts.summary: Stretch receptors report blood pressure to the cardiovascular centre, which adjusts the heart and vessels to bring it back.

misconceptions: Learners think homeostasis means a value never changes. The textbook calls it a dynamic state of balance within limits, and core temperature is given as a range of 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius.
Learners hear 'negative' as 'bad'. Negative feedback opposes a change, and it is the common method of regulation in the body.
Learners think positive feedback is the good kind. It amplifies a change, and the textbook's example is brief and ends with the birth.
sequence: Each cell contributes to homeostasis; a parameter far out of range means illness.
Temperature as the clearest loop: range, detector, correction in each direction.
Negative feedback stated generally, with the hormone example that switches itself off.
Blood pressure: baroreceptors, the cardiovascular centre, and the correction in each direction.
Positive feedback: oxytocin and labour, and why it is rare and self-ending.
examples: Core temperature stays at about 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius (97.7 to 99.5 degrees Fahrenheit) even when the surroundings are very different.
If the temperature is too high the body increases blood flow to the skin and sweats; if it falls below the set core temperature, shivering and thyroid hormone raise heat production.
When blood pressure rises, baroreceptors fire faster, the heart is slowed and the vessels widen; when it drops, the opposite happens.

figures.shows: A feedback loop with boxes for stimulus, sensor, control centre and effector, drawn for body temperature, with a toggle to show the loop for 'too hot' and for 'too cold'.
figures.learnerAction: Click through the loop and say which way the effector pushes.

figures.shows: A line of blood pressure over a few minutes that rises, then falls back toward its starting level, with a second line of baroreceptor firing rate that rises and falls with it, shown as described values.
figures.learnerAction: Predict the direction of the heart rate line before it is revealed.

questionPlan.sample: Core temperature is held at about 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius. A reading is 38.1. By how many degrees does it exceed the top of the range?
Order the baroreceptor reflex after blood pressure rises too high.
answer: The baroreceptors are stretched more tightly and fire at a higher rate
The cardiovascular centre receives the signal and triggers a reflex
Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart rises and sympathetic stimulation of the arterioles falls
Cardiac output falls and the vessels widen

questionPlan.sample: Sort each example: sweating when the core temperature is too high; shivering when it falls below the set value; glucocorticoid release that eases off as blood levels rise; oxytocin release that intensifies labour contractions; baroreceptors lowering a raised blood pressure.
questionPlan.answer: Negative feedback: sweating, shivering, glucocorticoid release easing off, baroreceptor lowering of pressure. Positive feedback: oxytocin and labour contractions.

questionPlan.sample: Which description of homeostasis matches the textbook?
choices: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life
A state in which every measurement stays fixed
A response that always makes a change larger
The temperature of the surrounding air
questionPlan.answer: A dynamic state of balance within parameters that are compatible with life

lessons.title: Bones and muscles
lessons.objective: Describe how bone is constantly rebuilt and how muscle contracts using ATP, and say what use and disuse do to each, with the WHO's physical activity figure read correctly.

concepts.title: Bone remodelling
concepts.summary: Osteoblasts form new bone while osteoclasts break down old bone, and the balance between them constantly reshapes it.

concepts.title: Osteoporosis
concepts.summary: A decrease in bone mass that occurs when the rate of bone resorption exceeds the rate of bone formation.

concepts.title: Muscle contraction
concepts.summary: In skeletal and cardiac muscle, myosin pulls on actin once calcium ions expose binding sites, and the process needs ATP.

concepts.title: Hypertrophy and atrophy
concepts.summary: More sarcomeres and myofibrils in each fibre with training, or fewer with disuse; the number of fibres does not change.

concepts.title: Relative risk
concepts.summary: A statement such as a 20 to 30 percent increased risk compares one group with another and is not a count of deaths.

misconceptions: Learners think bone is inert once grown. It is dynamic, with new tissue formed and old tissue dissolved all the time.
Learners think training adds muscle fibres. The number of fibres is genetically determined; what changes is the amount of sarcomeres and myofibrils inside them.
Learners read '20 to 30 percent increased risk' as 20 to 30 percentage points. It is a proportional increase on the baseline risk.
sequence: Bone as living tissue: osteogenic cells, osteoblasts, osteoclasts.
Balance and its failure: osteoporosis.
Muscle contraction in one paragraph: actin, myosin, calcium, ATP.
Use and disuse: hypertrophy, atrophy, a limb in a cast.
What exercise does for bone density, with resistance training stronger than other types.
Reading the WHO's relative risk for people who are insufficiently active.
examples: A limb in a cast shows atrophied muscles when the cast comes off.
Hypothetical baseline: if 50 in 1,000 sufficiently active adults die over a period, a 20 to 30 percent higher risk means 60 to 65 in 1,000 for a comparable insufficiently active group.

figures.shows: A bone surface with an osteoblast laying down tissue and an osteoclast removing it, with a balance beam that tips as the learner changes the relative activity of the two cells.
figures.learnerAction: Tip the balance to show formation ahead of, equal to, and behind resorption and read the label that appears.

figures.shows: A sarcomere in two states, relaxed and contracted, with calcium and ATP as switches.
figures.learnerAction: Switch calcium and ATP on and off and watch whether the filaments pull.

questionPlan.sample: A person's leg looks thinner after weeks in a cast. According to the textbook, what has happened inside the muscle?
choices: Each fibre has lost sarcomeres and myofibrils, but the number of fibres is unchanged
Many muscle fibres have died and been replaced by fat
The muscle has turned into tendon
Nothing, because the number of fibres falls only with age
questionPlan.answer: Each fibre has lost sarcomeres and myofibrils, but the number of fibres is unchanged

questionPlan.sample: Osteoporosis is described as a disease in which:
choices: osteoblasts break down bone faster than osteoclasts form it
calcium is stored in muscle instead of bone
questionPlan.answer: bone resorption exceeds bone formation

questionPlan.sample: Suppose, for a made up example, 50 in 1,000 sufficiently active adults die during a study period. The WHO says insufficiently active people have a 20 to 30 percent increased risk of death compared with sufficiently active people. What is the highest number of deaths per 1,000 you would expect in a comparable insufficiently active group?
The bone cell that breaks bone down is called an ___.
questionPlan.answer: osteoclast

lessons.title: The heart
lessons.objective: Follow blood through the four chambers and the two circuits, calculate cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume, and say what exercise does to heart rate and output.

concepts.title: Four chambers
concepts.summary: Two upper receiving chambers, the atria, and two lower pumping chambers, the ventricles, one pair on each side.

concepts.title: Pulmonary and systemic circuits
concepts.summary: The pulmonary circuit takes blood to and from the lungs; the systemic circuit takes oxygenated blood to the tissues and returns it.

concepts.title: Cardiac output
concepts.summary: The amount of blood pumped by each ventricle in one minute: stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.

concepts.title: Resting heart rate
concepts.summary: 60 to 100 beats per minute for a normal adult; below 60 is bradycardia and above 100 is tachycardia.

misconceptions: Learners think the left and right sides mix blood. They are two pumps in series, each ejecting about the same volume per beat.

Learners think every vein carries deoxygenated blood and every artery oxygenated blood. The pulmonary circuit reverses the usual picture, so define arteries and veins by the direction of flow, not by oxygen.

Learners think a resting rate under 60 always means disease. The textbook says trained athletes typically have very low rates and that, without other symptoms, bradycardia is not considered clinically significant.
sequence: The fist-sized pump and its two jobs.
Four chambers and which two receive and which two pump.
The path of blood as one loop: right atrium, right ventricle, lungs, left atrium, left ventricle, body, back to the right atrium.
Cardiac output as a product, worked with resting numbers.
Exercise: heart rate up to 150, stroke volume up to about 130 mL, output about 19.5 litres a minute.
Reading a resting rate against 60 to 100, with athletes as the exception, and the WHO's 150 minutes figure as the health link.
examples: Resting adult: 70 mL per beat at 75 beats per minute gives 5,250 mL, or 5.25 litres, a minute.
Healthy young adult in exercise: 130 mL per beat at 150 beats per minute gives 19,500 mL, or 19.5 litres, a minute.
A resting rate of 54 beats per minute in a trained athlete with no symptoms.

figures.shows: A flat diagram of the heart with four chambers and the two circuits, blood path steppable one chamber at a time, vessels unlabelled until the learner places them.
figures.learnerAction: Step through the path, placing each label before it appears.

figures.shows: Stroke volume and heart rate as two inputs, cardiac output as the output in litres a minute.
figures.learnerAction: Enter a stroke volume and a rate and read the output.

questionPlan.sample: Order one trip of blood, starting in the right atrium.
A resting adult's ventricle ejects 70 mL a beat at 75 beats per minute. What is the cardiac output in litres per minute?
During exercise a healthy young adult's heart rate is 150 beats per minute and stroke volume is 130 mL. What is the cardiac output in litres per minute?
A trained athlete, with no symptoms, has a resting rate of 54 beats per minute. What does the textbook say about a rate like this?
choices: Trained athletes typically have very low rates, and with no other symptoms it is not considered clinically significant
Any rate under 60 shows the heart is failing
It is normal only for children
It is the same as tachycardia
questionPlan.answer: Trained athletes typically have very low rates, and with no other symptoms it is not considered clinically significant

questionPlan.sample: A resting heart rate above 100 beats per minute is called ___.
questionPlan.answer: tachycardia

lessons.title: Blood vessels and blood pressure
lessons.objective: Put the vessels in order along the path of blood, read a blood pressure as systolic over diastolic, and describe how clinics and home checks use thresholds without treating one reading as a diagnosis.

concepts.title: Blood
concepts.summary: A connective tissue with formed elements (red cells, white cells, platelets) suspended in the fluid plasma.

concepts.title: Arteries, capillaries and veins
concepts.summary: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, capillaries exchange nutrients and wastes, and veins return blood to the heart.

concepts.title: Systolic and diastolic pressure
concepts.summary: The higher number is the pressure when the ventricles contract; the lower is the pressure when they relax.

concepts.title: High blood pressure
concepts.summary: Pressure in the blood vessels that stays too high; it usually causes no symptoms and is found only by measuring.

misconceptions: Learners think high blood pressure announces itself. NHS and WHO both say it usually causes no symptoms, so the only way to know is to measure.
Learners think one high reading is a diagnosis. NHS describes repeat and home or 24 hour monitoring to confirm, and WHO diagnoses on readings from two different days.

Learners think the thresholds are one universal number. The pack gives 140/90 in a clinic and 135/85 at home (NHS), and 140/90 on readings from two different days (WHO). The setting and the number of readings matter.
sequence: What blood is made of, in one paragraph.
The path through the vessels: artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, vein.
What a blood pressure reading measures and what the two numbers mean.
Taking a reading: the cuff and the thresholds, in clinic and at home.
Why one reading is not a diagnosis, and what confirms it.
Risk factors that can and cannot be changed, and why symptoms are a poor guide.
examples: A reading of 120/80: the systolic pressure is the higher value and reflects ejection of blood during ventricular contraction, the diastolic is the lower value during relaxation; the two differ by 40.
A clinic reading of 152/96 is above the 140/90 threshold, so the next step described by NHS and WHO is confirmation by repeat readings, not a conclusion.
A home reading of 118/76 is below the 135/85 home threshold.

figures.shows: A pressure trace in described form: a repeating rise to a peak and fall to a trough, with the peak and the trough marked by two cursors the learner can drag to read as 'over' numbers.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the cursors to read the systolic and diastolic values.

figures.shows: Source, setting, number: NHS clinic 140/90, NHS home 135/85, WHO diagnosis 140/90 on readings from two different days.
figures.learnerAction: Match a given reading to the rows it meets.
figures.placement: Thresholds section, after the reading question.

questionPlan.sample: Order the vessels along the path blood takes from the heart and back.
In a reading of 120/80, the first number is the ___ pressure.
questionPlan.answer: systolic

questionPlan.sample: A blood pressure reads 120/80. What is the difference between the two numbers?
At what home reading does NHS say you are usually considered to have high blood pressure?
questionPlan.answer: 135/85 or higher

questionPlan.sample: A clinic reading of 152/96 is above the usual threshold. What do NHS and WHO describe as the next step in finding out whether someone has high blood pressure?
choices: Repeat readings, such as home checks, a return visit or 24 hour monitoring, or readings on two different days
None, because one reading is enough to diagnose
questionPlan.answer: Repeat readings, such as home checks, a return visit or 24 hour monitoring, or readings on two different days

questionPlan.sample: Sort each WHO risk factor for high blood pressure: excessive salt; physical inactivity; tobacco; family history; age over 65; co-existing diabetes or kidney disease.
questionPlan.answer: Modifiable: excessive salt, physical inactivity, tobacco. Non-modifiable: family history, age over 65, co-existing diabetes or kidney disease.

lessons.title: Lungs and breathing
lessons.objective: Explain how pressure differences move air in and out, how oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane, and how a respiratory rate is read against the normal ranges.

concepts.title: Respiratory membrane
concepts.summary: The alveolar wall and the capillary wall together, about 0.5 micrometres thick, across which gases pass by simple diffusion.

concepts.title: Pulmonary ventilation
concepts.summary: Movement of air into and out of the lungs, driven by pressure differences made by the diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs.

concepts.title: Passive expiration
concepts.summary: Normal breathing out needs no muscular energy; the lungs recoil as the muscles relax.

concepts.title: Respiratory rate
concepts.summary: Breaths per minute; 12 to 18 for an adolescent or adult, and higher in young children.

misconceptions: Learners think the lungs pull air in by themselves. The lungs are passive; the diaphragm and intercostal muscles make the pressure changes.
Learners think breathing out needs effort. Normal expiration is passive.
Learners think breathing is driven by low oxygen. The respiratory centre in the medulla responds to carbon dioxide, oxygen and pH levels in the blood.
sequence: What the lungs are for: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out.
The respiratory membrane and why it is so thin.
A breath in: muscles contract, volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in.
A breath out, passively.
Rate: the ranges by age, and what a rate can show.
The MedlinePlus lung disease summary: the number of breaths in a day and what lung disease covers.
Health link: second-hand smoke and a relative risk read correctly.
examples: The respiratory membrane is 0.5 micrometres thick, which is 0.0005 millimetres.
'Nearly 25,000 breaths a day' (MedlinePlus) corresponds to about 17 breaths a minute, since 25,000 divided by 1,440 minutes is about 17.4.
An adult counts 24 breaths in a minute: above the 12 to 18 range given for adolescents and adults.

figures.shows: A side view of the chest with the diaphragm, rib muscles, lung and a pressure gauge, in two switchable views, breathing in and breathing out.
figures.learnerAction: Switch views and say whether the gauge reads above or below atmospheric pressure.
figures.placement: A breath in and a breath out.

figures.shows: Age band and normal respiratory rate: under 1 year 30 to 60; about 10 years 18 to 30; adolescent and adult 12 to 18.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Order a normal breath out.
answer: The diaphragm and rib muscles relax
The chest cavity and lungs decrease in volume
The pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure

questionPlan.sample: The respiratory membrane is about 0.5 micrometres thick. How many millimetres is that? (1 millimetre is 1,000 micrometres.)
A resting adult counts 24 breaths in one minute. Compared with the range the textbook gives for adolescents and adults, this is:
choices: the normal rate for a 10 year old child
questionPlan.answer: above the range of 12 to 18

questionPlan.sample: MedlinePlus says you breathe nearly 25,000 times in a normal day. About how many breaths a minute is that, to the nearest whole number?

OpenStax says the risk of lung cancer is increased by up to 30 percent in nonsmokers who live with a smoker. For a made up baseline of 10 in 1,000 nonsmokers, what number in 1,000 does an increase of 30 percent give?
Why does normal breathing out need no muscular effort?
choices: The lungs recoil as the diaphragm and rib muscles relax
The diaphragm pushes air out hard
questionPlan.answer: The lungs recoil as the diaphragm and rib muscles relax

lessons.title: Digestion
lessons.objective: Follow food along the alimentary canal, separate propulsion, mixing, chemical digestion and absorption, and explain why the small intestine is where most absorption happens and what lactose intolerance shows about enzymes.

concepts.title: Alimentary canal
concepts.summary: A one-way tube from the mouth to the anus, modified as the pharynx, esophagus, stomach and the small and large intestines.

concepts.title: Propulsion and peristalsis
concepts.summary: Swallowing is voluntary; peristalsis is the involuntary sequence of alternating waves of contraction and relaxation that moves food along and mixes it.

concepts.title: Absorption
concepts.summary: Broken-down nutrients pass from the canal into the bloodstream or, for lipids, into lacteals, mainly in the small intestine.

concepts.title: Folds, villi and microvilli
concepts.summary: Three features of the lining that increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine more than 600-fold.

concepts.title: Lactase
concepts.summary: The enzyme that digests the milk sugar lactose; too little of it leads to lactose intolerance.

misconceptions: Learners think the stomach does all the digesting. It mainly holds food and releases small amounts into the small intestine, which is where most digestion and practically all absorption occur.
Learners think food inside the canal is already inside the body. Food and waste in the canal are technically outside the body until nutrients are absorbed.
Learners think food is processed in the order eaten. In the stomach it is mixed with digestive juices into chyme.
sequence: A tube from mouth to anus, open at both ends: why food in it is technically outside the body.
Swallowing and peristalsis: propulsion and mixing.
The stomach as a holding chamber and chyme.
Absorption in the small intestine and the three features that enlarge the surface.
Lactose intolerance as a case of a missing enzyme.
examples: Peristalsis is strong enough that food and liquid reach the stomach even when a person stands on their head.
A person who gets cramps and gas after dairy may have absorptive cells making too little lactase.

figures.shows: A simplified body outline with the canal organs unlabelled and a switchable view that adds names and one-line jobs.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each name onto its organ in order from the mouth.

figures.shows: A cross-section of the small intestine wall with circular folds, villi and microvilli drawn at three zoom levels.
figures.learnerAction: Zoom through the three levels and say what each one adds to the surface.

questionPlan.sample: Order the parts of the alimentary canal that food passes through, from first to last.

Sort each event: the tongue and pharyngeal muscles push food into the esophagus; waves of contraction mix food with juices in the stomach; nutrients cross the lining into the bloodstream; the stomach releases small amounts of chyme into the small intestine.
questionPlan.answer: Propulsion: pushing food into the esophagus. Mixing: waves of contraction in the stomach. Absorption: nutrients crossing the lining. Controlled release: chyme released in small amounts.

questionPlan.sample: Someone has indigestion after eating dairy products. Which explanation matches the textbook's account of lactose intolerance?
choices: The absorptive cells of the small intestine do not produce enough lactase to digest lactose
The stomach makes too much acid
questionPlan.answer: The absorptive cells of the small intestine do not produce enough lactase to digest lactose

questionPlan.sample: Which three features increase the absorptive surface of the small intestine by more than 600-fold?
questionPlan.answer: Circular folds, villi and microvilli

lessons.title: Nutrition and energy
lessons.objective: Trace how food becomes ATP, read an energy budget split of 70, 20 and 10 percent, and use the WHO's four principles and its sugar and salt limits to judge a day's food, without personal dietary advice.

concepts.title: ATP from glucose
concepts.summary: Glucose from digested carbohydrate is taken up by cells in response to insulin and broken down by glycolysis to make ATP.

concepts.title: Basal metabolic rate
concepts.summary: The daily energy used at rest; about 70 percent of daily expenditure goes to basic organ functions, 20 percent to physical activity and 10 percent to temperature control.

concepts.title: Nutritional Calorie
concepts.summary: The heat needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 degree Celsius, which differs from the physics calorie.

concepts.title: Four principles of a healthy diet
concepts.summary: Adequacy, balance, moderation and diversity (WHO).

misconceptions: Learners think most energy goes into exercise. The textbook gives about 70 percent to basic organ functions at rest.
Learners confuse calorie and Calorie. The nutritional Calorie is the larger unit.
Learners treat nutrition as one rule about one nutrient. WHO frames healthy diets with four principles that apply together, and says the exact make-up varies with age, culture and available food.
sequence: Energy as ATP and where glucose comes from.
Units: the nutritional Calorie.
Where daily energy goes: 70, 20 and 10 percent.
The WHO's four principles of a healthy diet.
Two limits as worked numbers: free sugars under 10 percent of energy, salt under 5 grams.
Link back: salt and blood pressure, from the blood pressure lesson.
examples: A 2,000 Calorie day: 10 percent is 200 Calories from free sugars at most, which WHO equates to about 50 grams.
A day of 2,200 Calories: 70 percent is 1,540 on basic functions, 20 percent is 440 on activity and 10 percent is 220 on temperature control.
A recipe with 2.4 grams of salt a portion reaches WHO's 5 gram limit after two portions with 0.2 grams to spare.

figures.shows: A single bar split 70, 20 and 10 into organ functions, physical activity and temperature control, each a different tone.
figures.learnerAction: Enter a daily total and read the three parts.

figures.shows: The four WHO principles with a one-line meaning each.
figures.learnerAction: none
figures.placement: Healthy diet section, after the sort question.

questionPlan.sample: Order how carbohydrate becomes ATP.
answer: Digestion breaks polysaccharides into monosaccharides including glucose
Glucose is transported across the wall of the small intestine into the circulation
The liver passes glucose on or stores the excess as glycogen
Cells take up circulating glucose in response to insulin
Glycolysis transfers some of the energy in glucose to make ATP

questionPlan.sample: A person uses 2,200 Calories a day. About 20 percent goes to physical activity. How many Calories is that?
WHO says free sugars should be under 10 percent of total daily energy. On a 2,000 Calorie day, how many Calories is 10 percent?
WHO sets an adult limit of less than 5 grams of salt a day. One portion of a dish has 2.4 grams. How many whole portions stay within the limit if the dish were the only source?

Match each statement to a WHO principle: meets needs without exceeding them; energy intake matches energy expenditure; limited intake of things that may be detrimental; a wide variety of nutritious foods.
questionPlan.answer: Adequacy: meets needs without exceeding them. Balance: energy intake matches expenditure. Moderation: limited intake of detrimental things. Diversity: a wide variety of nutritious foods.

lessons.title: Kidneys and water balance
lessons.objective: Describe filtration and reabsorption in the nephron, use the 180 litres a day and 99 percent figures to find the daily urine volume, and explain how ADH changes the urine.

concepts.title: Nephron
concepts.summary: One of about a million tiny structures in each kidney that filter the blood, removing wastes and extra water as urine.

concepts.title: Glomerular filtration rate
concepts.summary: The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute; about 125 mL a minute in males and 105 mL in females, which is about 180 and 150 litres a day.

concepts.title: Reabsorption
concepts.summary: About 99 percent of the filtrate returns to the circulation, leaving 1 to 2 litres of urine a day.

concepts.title: ADH and aquaporins
concepts.summary: ADH inserts water channels in the collecting ducts; more ADH gives more concentrated urine and less gives dilute urine.

concepts.title: Other kidney jobs
concepts.summary: Regulating pH, helping control blood pressure, making most of the body's erythropoietin and finishing the activation of vitamin D.

misconceptions: Learners think the kidneys only produce urine. The textbook lists pH, blood pressure, red blood cell production and vitamin D as well.
Learners think urine is what is left when the kidney filters a little blood. The kidneys filter about 180 litres a day and return nearly all of it.
Learners think more water drunk always means more ADH. ADH rises when blood is too concentrated and falls when it is dilute.
sequence: Two kidneys, the nephron and the path of urine.
Filtration at 180 litres a day and the 99 percent that comes back.
How ADH sets how much water is recovered.
Hormones and thirst keeping total body water steady.
Beyond urine: pH, pressure, red cells and vitamin D.
Health link: diabetes, high blood pressure and family history as risks for kidney disease.
examples: 125 mL a minute for 1,440 minutes is 180,000 mL, or 180 litres; with 99 percent reabsorbed, 1 percent of 180 litres leaves 1.8 litres of urine.
A kidney with less ADH around: fewer water channels, less water recovered, dilute urine.

figures.shows: A nephron drawn as a tube with the filter at one end and the collecting duct at the other, with a water meter that shows how much of 180 litres remains at each stage as the learner steps through.
figures.learnerAction: Step through and read the water remaining at each stage.

figures.shows: A collecting duct with and without water channels (two views).
figures.learnerAction: Switch ADH on and off and say which way the urine goes.

questionPlan.sample: The kidneys filter about 180 litres a day and about 99 percent is reabsorbed. How many litres of urine is that?
A glomerular filtration rate of 125 mL a minute: how many litres of filtrate in a day? (1,440 minutes in a day.)
Order the path from filtering to leaving the body.
answer: Wastes and extra water become urine

questionPlan.sample: Less ADH is released. What happens to the urine?
choices: Fewer water channels are inserted, less water is recovered, and the urine is dilute
More water is recovered and the urine is concentrated
questionPlan.answer: Fewer water channels are inserted, less water is recovered, and the urine is dilute

questionPlan.sample: Which of these does MedlinePlus list as raising the risk of kidney disease?
choices: Diabetes, high blood pressure, or a close family member with kidney disease
questionPlan.answer: Diabetes, high blood pressure, or a close family member with kidney disease

lessons.title: Nerves and senses
lessons.objective: Describe an action potential from a described voltage graph, follow a signal across a synapse and through a reflex arc, and say what happens to signalling when myelin is damaged.

concepts.title: Action potential
concepts.summary: A brief electrical signal in which the membrane potential rises from about -70 mV, reaches about +30 mV and returns.

concepts.title: Chemical synapse
concepts.summary: A neurotransmitter released from one cell crosses a small gap and binds to receptors on the next cell.

concepts.title: Sensory receptor and transduction
concepts.summary: Specialised receptor cells change the stimulus into a change in membrane potential.

concepts.title: Reflex arc
concepts.summary: Sensory input, central processing at a synapse in the spinal cord, and motor output, as in withdrawing a hand from a hot stove.

concepts.title: Demyelination
concepts.summary: Loss of the insulation around axons, as in multiple sclerosis, an autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system.

misconceptions: Learners think a nerve signal is like current in a wire. It is a membrane voltage change carried by ions entering and leaving, and the signal at a synapse is chemical.
Learners think the reflex goes to the brain first. In the textbook's example the synapse is in the spinal cord.
Learners think multiple sclerosis is a disease of muscles. It is an autoimmune attack on myelin in the central nervous system.
sequence: The resting membrane at -70 mV.
Depolarisation to +30 mV, repolarisation and return, as a graph in words.
Passing the signal on at a synapse.
Receptors and transduction: how stimuli start signals.
A reflex arc from stove to hand.
Health link: what losing the insulation does, as in multiple sclerosis, and what a reduced sense of smell can change about salt.
Note: the pack covers receptors in general and smell in this list; taste, vision and hearing are not supported by the listed passages.
examples: Sodium is about ten times more concentrated outside the cell than inside, so opening sodium channels sends the voltage toward zero.
Voltage swing: from -70 mV to +30 mV is 100 mV.
A hand on a hot stove: painful stimulus, synapse in the spinal cord, motor neuron, biceps contracts.
Loss of the sense of smell can make food taste bland, and the textbook links age-related loss of smell to people salting food more, which can raise blood volume and blood pressure.

figures.shows: A voltage against time trace, shown as values: rest at -70, rise to +30, fall back to -70, with labelled stages hidden until chosen.
figures.learnerAction: Click the stretch of the trace that matches each named stage.

figures.shows: A synapse with vesicles, cleft and receptors, steppable.
figures.learnerAction: Step through and order the events.

questionPlan.sample: An action potential starts at -70 mV and peaks at +30 mV. By how many millivolts does the membrane potential rise?
On the trace, the voltage moves from +30 mV back toward -70 mV. Which process is that, and which ion mainly leaves the cell?
questionPlan.answer: Repolarisation, with potassium leaving

questionPlan.sample: Order the events at a chemical synapse.
answer: An action potential reaches the axon terminal
Vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft
Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the next cell

questionPlan.sample: Order a withdrawal reflex from a hot stove.
answer: A painful stimulus acts on a sensory receptor
The sensory signal reaches a synapse in the spinal cord
A ventral motor neuron is activated
The biceps contracts and the arm withdraws

questionPlan.sample: The change of a stimulus into a change in membrane potential is called ___.
questionPlan.answer: transduction

lessons.title: Hormones and blood sugar
lessons.objective: Explain how hormones reach only their target cells, how insulin and glucagon hold blood glucose between 70 and 100 mg/dL, what goes wrong in type 2 diabetes, and what the WHO lists for prevention.

concepts.title: Hormone and target cell
concepts.summary: A hormone travels in the blood but affects only cells with receptors for it.

concepts.title: Insulin and glucagon
concepts.summary: Insulin, from beta cells, lowers blood glucose; glucagon, from alpha cells, raises it; each is switched off as the level moves back.

concepts.title: Type 2 diabetes
concepts.summary: Cells become resistant to insulin, the pancreas makes more, and over time the beta cells become exhausted.

concepts.title: Early signs of diabetes
concepts.summary: Excessive urination and thirst, because glucose in the filtrate draws water into the urine.

concepts.title: Prevention of type 2 diabetes
concepts.summary: WHO lists a healthy body weight, at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week, a healthy diet that avoids sugar and saturated fat, and not smoking.

misconceptions: Learners think insulin is only a diabetes drug. It is a hormone made in the pancreas by everyone.
Learners think type 2 diabetes means no insulin. The textbook says the cells resist insulin and the pancreas first increases its output.
Learners think high blood sugar is felt at once. WHO says type 2 symptoms can be mild and take years to notice, so diagnosis can come after complications have arisen.
sequence: Hormones and target cells.
Blood glucose as a controlled value: 70 to 100 mg/dL and the two hormones.
A meal and the insulin response.
Type 2 diabetes: resistance, exhaustion, and why thirst and frequent urination follow.
What damage high glucose does over time, and what WHO lists for prevention.
Note on units: the pack gives mg/dL only.
examples: Blood glucose rises above 70 to 100 mg/dL, insulin is released, cells take up glucose, and the level returns.
In a group of 400 people with diabetes mellitus, about 95 percent, or 380, would have type 2.

figures.shows: A glucose line that rises after a meal and falls back toward the 70 to 100 band, with an insulin line that peaks just behind it, as described values.
figures.learnerAction: Predict where the glucagon line would sit when glucose dips below the band.

figures.shows: A feedback loop for blood glucose: stimulus, pancreas, hormone, target cells, with a toggle between the high and low cases.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the case and name the hormone.

questionPlan.sample: Blood glucose rises above the usual range. Which hormone is released?
questionPlan.answer: Insulin

questionPlan.sample: Order what happens after a meal.
answer: Carbohydrate is absorbed and blood glucose rises above the range
Body cells take up glucose from the blood
Blood glucose returns toward the range and insulin release is inhibited

questionPlan.sample: Order how high blood glucose leads to thirst.
answer: The kidneys filter glucose and the excess draws water into the urine
The person passes large amounts of urine
The body loses water and the person is continually thirsty

questionPlan.sample: Type 2 diabetes is about 95 percent of all cases. In a group of 400 people with diabetes mellitus, about how many have type 2?
Which of these is NOT on the WHO's list of ways to prevent or delay type 2 diabetes?
choices: At least 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week
questionPlan.answer: Taking a daily vitamin supplement

lessons.title: The immune system and vaccines
lessons.objective: Separate innate from adaptive immunity, explain why a second exposure gives a stronger and faster response, say what a vaccine is, and read vaccination coverage figures.

concepts.title: Innate and adaptive responses
concepts.summary: The innate response is rapid but nonspecific; the adaptive response is slower at a first infection but highly specific and effective.

concepts.title: Antibody and antigen
concepts.summary: An antibody is a protein made by B cells that binds a specific antigen, a structure on the surface of a pathogen.

concepts.title: Immunological memory
concepts.summary: On re-exposure the secondary response is stronger and faster, often clearing the pathogen before any symptoms.

concepts.title: Vaccine
concepts.summary: A killed or weakened pathogen, or its components, that builds immunological memory without causing much in the way of symptoms.

concepts.title: Vaccination coverage
concepts.summary: The share of a group that has received doses; WHO reports it by vaccine and year.

misconceptions: Learners think a vaccine gives the disease. A vaccine uses a killed or weakened pathogen or its components to build memory without causing much in the way of symptoms.
Learners think one flu vaccine works for ever. Viruses such as influenza mutate their surface molecules, so a new formulation is made each season.
Learners think immunity is all or nothing and the same everywhere. WHO coverage figures differ by vaccine and by region, which is why the lesson reads numbers and does not assert a general rule.
sequence: Two overlapping defences: innate, then adaptive.
B cells, antibodies and antigens.
Primary and secondary responses as a graph in words.
What a vaccine is and what it borrows from the primary response.
Why the flu vaccine changes each year.
Reading WHO coverage figures for measles, and how to find your own national schedule.
examples: Measles: 84 percent of children had one dose by their second birthday and 77 percent had two (end of 2025, WHO), so 16 in every 100 had not had a first dose.
A graph described in words: after a first exposure antibody level rises slowly and stays low; after a second, it rises faster and higher.
NHS pages list flu vaccine for people at higher risk, including adults aged 65 and over; the lesson cites this as an example of a schedule and does not tell the learner what they personally need.

figures.shows: Two antibody curves against time, described as values: first exposure rises late to a low peak, second exposure rises early to a high peak.
figures.learnerAction: Choose which curve belongs to the first exposure and which to the second.

figures.shows: Vaccine, share covered in 2025: DTP3 85 percent; first measles dose 84 percent; second measles dose 77 percent; first HPV dose in girls 33 percent.
figures.learnerAction: none

questionPlan.sample: Sort each feature: rapid but nonspecific; slower at first infection but highly specific; produces antibodies through B cells; gives a stronger, faster second response.
questionPlan.answer: Innate: rapid but nonspecific. Adaptive: slower at first but highly specific, antibodies through B cells, stronger and faster second response.

questionPlan.sample: Two antibody curves are shown. One rises late to a low peak. The other rises early to a high peak. Which curve shows the second exposure to the same pathogen?
choices: Neither; the curves show different pathogens
questionPlan.answer: The early, high one

questionPlan.sample: The textbook defines a vaccine as:
choices: a killed or weakened pathogen or its components that leads to immunological memory without causing much in the way of symptoms
a drug that kills pathogens directly
a dose of antibodies taken from another person
a cream that blocks infection on the skin
questionPlan.answer: a killed or weakened pathogen or its components that leads to immunological memory without causing much in the way of symptoms

questionPlan.sample: WHO reports that 84 percent of children had received one dose of measles vaccine by their second birthday. Out of 1,000 children, how many had not?
A protein made by B cells that binds a specific antigen is an ___.
questionPlan.answer: antibody

questionPlan.sample: Find your own country's vaccination schedule and note which vaccines it lists for adults. (Self-rated; the course does not say what any person needs.)
questionPlan.answer: self-rated

courseCheck: A mixed check, all markable without free text: sort tissue jobs and feedback examples; order the baroreceptor reflex, the path of blood, the vessels, a breath out, the canal, food to ATP, the path of urine, a synapse and a reflex arc; compute cardiac output, the excess over a range, filtration and urine volume, an energy budget share and a relative risk; read a blood pressure, a respiratory rate, a resting heart rate and a vaccination coverage figure against the stated ranges; choose the definition of homeostasis, osteoporosis, a vaccine and a type 2 diabetes prevention measure. Include one statement that the course explains how the body works and is not medical advice.
platformNeeds: A reading-against-a-range figure: a gauge with a shaded band where the learner places a value (temperature, blood pressure, resting heart rate, respiratory rate, blood glucose) and sees only whether it is inside or outside. Fallback: data_series with a marked band.
A feedback loop builder with stimulus, sensor, control centre and effector slots, filled by the learner for temperature, blood pressure and blood glucose. Fallback: svg_figure with switchable views.

A source tag on every number that comes from a health body (for example 'NHS, page reviewed 19 July 2024') and a unit and region note where thresholds or units differ (mmHg, mg/dL and mmol/L, national schedules). The first-aid course asks for the same kind of tag.

One persistent line on health lessons stating that the lesson explains how the body works and does not give personal medical advice, shown once per lesson. Fallback: put it in each lesson's closing recap.
A heart and circulation stepper in which the learner places labels before they appear, as in lesson 4. Fallback: svg_figure with switchable views.
unverified: Every source was read from the pack's saved text, fetched on 2026-11-14. No page was reopened live for this plan.
The licence for OpenStax is recorded in the words of index.json, which does not give a version number. The brief for the pack assumed CC BY 4.0; the pages say NonCommercial-ShareAlike.
The teaching labels sensor, control centre and effector (lesson 2) are not in the pack's passages.
Whether the NHS 140/90 and 135/85 thresholds need both numbers or either one to be met is not stated on the NHS page. The lesson uses only clear cases.

Whether the MedlinePlus lung and kidney summaries remain public domain depends on the policy page statement (policy-medlineplus-using-content lines 59 to 72); the individual pages show only 'Copyright' in the footer.
Several OpenStax figures disagree with each other or with simple arithmetic (see plan-notes.md, Gaps and conflicts). The lessons use the figures that check out.
